#2680. JJ Redick is encouraging the Lakers to foul more

Embracing contact and physicality is paramount to being a good-to-great defensive unit. The Los Angeles Lakers intend to become a good-to-great defensive unit, so they can properly complement their league-leading offense and compete for a title this season.

Currently, they're middling and sit 15th in defensive rating, including 11th over their eight-game winning streak, per Cleaning the Glass. Head coach JJ Redick wants his players to assume a hard-nosed identity, even to the point of fouling — at least in certain contexts.

"We encourage physicality. We encourage – if we're not in the bonus and somebody goes to follow and they go to set the on-ball screen to ghost or touch roll, just two-hand shove them…We encourage that," Redick told reporters prior to Sunday's win over the Phoenix Suns. "The biggest thing for us is being smart about when we're fouling and right now we're giving up 6.1 free throws per game on non-shooting fouls in the bonus and that's entirely too many. I think that's bottom third in the NBA right now so we're fouling too much in the bonus. But if we're not in the bonus, foul. That's good. That part doesn't bother me. Boxing out, whatever it may be, our physical players need to be physical and we're not going to tell them to play with handcuffs on."

The Lakers' propensity for putting opposing teams on the line with non-shooting fouls once they're in the bonus has hamstrung their defense. According to Cleaning the Glass, they're conceding a .247 free-throw rate to opponents, the 24th-worst mark in the league. During Redick's first two seasons as head coach of the Lakers, they touted one of the 10 lowest opposing free-throw rates both years.

Perhaps, that increased mark is the byproduct of Los Angeles generating an NBA-high 18.7% opponent turnover rate after finishing 15th in 2025-26 and 18th in 2024-25. Each of the top five in opponent turnover rate sports a bottom 10 opponent free-throw rate this season. Last year, three of the top five did. In 2024-25, six of the top seven were 20th or worse.

Moving forward, the Lakers will have to better balance these realities to fulfill Redick's wishes and build a physical-yet-discerning defense.

#2678. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2676. For the Seahawks this year, Drew Lock's numbers blow Sam Darnold's away

When Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald confirmed that Sam Darnold will start in Week 12 against the 49ers, assuming he is medically cleared, it was no surprise: The Seahawks signed Darnold to a three-year, $100 million contract last year and won the Super Bowl with Darnold at the helm. Quarterbacks like that don’t often get benched.

But Drew Lock has made it reasonable to question whether Darnold should get benched.

That’s because Lock has played three full games, and most of a fourth, while Darnold has missed time with injuries this season. And Lock hasn’t just been better than Darnold. Lock has been so much better that there’s no comparison between the two.

The Seahawks are 4-0 in the games when Lock was their primary quarterback. They’re 2-4 in the games with Darnold as the primary quarterback.

Of the 37 NFL quarterbacks who have thrown at least 90 passes this season, Lock ranks first with a passer rating of 125.6. Darnold ranks 31st with a passer rating of 79.5.

Lock has still not thrown an interception this season. Darnold has thrown nine.

Lock has completed 73.1 percent of his passes. Darnold has completed 60.2 percent.

Lock is averaging 9.0 yards per pass. Darnold is averaging 7.0 yards per pass.

Lock has been sacked on 5.1 percent of his dropbacks. Darnold has been sacked on 7.5 percent of his dropbacks.

With seven games left in the season, the 6-4 Seahawks are going to have a battle to get back to the playoffs. Macdonald believes Darnold is the best quarterback for the job. The numbers call that into question.

#2674. Texans OC Nick Caley weighs in on 'conservative play-calling' vs Browns

In Week 9 against the Los Angeles Chargers, the Houston Texans' offense was on fire with 44 total points. It looked like they were on their way to another blowout victory against the Cleveland Browns after jumping out to an early 17-0 lead.

However, the Texans' offense slowed down after that, giving up 20 straight points to Cleveland and failing to score again on offense until the fourth quarter. Houston ultimately lost 27-24, making it its fourth-largest blown lead in franchise history. After the loss, there were some criticisms that Texans offensive coordinator Nick Caley started to be conservative after getting the lead. However, he does not view it that way.

"I don't think overall, we just didn't get into a good rhythm. I thought the drive start, we didn't get really off to good drive starts," Caley said Monday. "Couple times we shot ourselves in the foot. Anytime you're going against good defense, an aggressive defense, on the road, I think it makes it harder. None of us did a good enough job starting first and foremost with me and clean it up and we're going to work hard to get that right."

After the loss, the Texans move to 3-6 and desperately need a win when they face the Indianapolis Colts on Thursday Night Football. Indianapolis is also sitting with just three wins, although they are coming off a victory against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday.

#2670. Oscar Piastri set for grid penalty at F1 Las Vegas GP

McLaren driver Oscar Piastri is set for a 10-place grid drop at F1's Las Vegas GP for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.

Piastri was already on the limit of four internal combustion engines for the year, but will need a fifth Mercedes V6 engine to finish the 2026 season.

As it is the first time he is exceeding his ICE allowance, the Australian will be docked 10 places on Las Vegas' starting grid.

"Oscar will take a new Internal Combustion Engine in Las Vegas after a reliability issue," the team said in its event preview. "As it is his fifth of the season, he will take a 10-place grid penalty, but he has a good chance to recover positions with overtaking in Saturday's race."

McLaren also confirmed it will take Mercedes' upgraded turbocharger, which the manufacturer developed under the FIA's so-called ADUO catch-up mechanism.

"Both cars, as with the other HPP-powered cars, will be fitted with a new ADUO-enabled turbo specification: the expected performance benefit is relatively small," McLaren noted.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren, Alexander Albon, Williams

#2667. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2661. Highs and lows of Fernando Mendoza’s starting debut for Las Vegas Raiders

Fernando Mendoza's first NFL start in the Las Vegas Raiders' Week 10 matchup against the Seattle Seahawks was a tale of two halves.

In the first half, he completed 11 of 13 passes for 90 yards, with both incompletions being throwaways, and had five rushes for 21 yards and a touchdown. According to Sumer Sports, that resulted in a total EPA of 6.56, an EPA per play of 0.328 and a 55 percent success rate — pretty good numbers. However, the second half was a different story, going six-for-16 with 53 passing yards and one rush for one yard to post a negative 13.49 total EPA, negative 0.642 EPA per play and a 14.3 percent success rate.

For the entire game, the No. 1 pick completed 17 of 29 passes (58.6 percent) for 143 passing yards, along with six rushes for 22 yards and a touchdown. That netted a negative 6.93 total EPA, negative 0.169 EPA per play and a 34.1 percent success rate.

For more context, Pro Football Focus credited him with a 66.7 percent adjusted completion percentage (accounting for the two throwaways and one drop), a slightly below-baseline (60.0) 59.8 passing grade and a slightly above-baseline rushing grade (65.2) to sit at a 62.2 overall mark.

While the numbers above help paint part of the picture, let's dive into the tape to see the full story.

To help get the rookie going, Klint Kubiak dialed up bootlegs on Mendoza's first three throws. The clip above is the third one and is a great decision by the quarterback.

His first read is to see if the go route from the outside receiver is available for a one-on-one opportunity. However, the Seahawks have that covered with the corner underneath and the boundary safety on top of the receiver to execute the Cover 2 side of the Cover 6 call.

Mendoza's next two options are either tight end Michael Mayer, who runs a chip release into a curl route, or wide receiver Jalen Nailor on a crossing/drag route. The MIKE linebacker is all over Mayer to take that away, and the WILL linebacker turns to ROBOT and help the corner against Nailor. Meanwhile, fullback Connor Heyward is working across the formation to sell the run fake and run a flat route.

Heyward gets contacted by the edge rusher, who ends up getting pressure on Mendoza. However, Mendoza does a good job of going through his reads, finding Heyward and throwing around the free rusher to dump it to the fullback, who picks up five on second and six to set up a third-and-short situation.

This isn't a sexy throw by any means, but it's a good process to put the offense in a favorable third down situation.

Here, we'll get a look at the touchdown run that got Allegiant Stadium rocking and is eerily similar to the run the Indiana product had to win the National Championship over Miami last January.

It's third and 10 as the Raiders come out in an empty formation where the Seahawks respond with a five-man box and both safeties deep pre-snap. That's the perfect look to run a quarterback draw into, and Mendoza sells it well by taking a drop with his first step and eyeing wide receivers Jalen Nailor and Tre Tucker post-snap, keeping the safeties in the end zone.

Then, he takes off and does a great job of setting up left guard Spencer Burford's block by getting downfield and pressing the five-yard line. That allows Burford to position himself between the linebacker and ball carrier. Finally, Mendoza shows off some impressive vision to see the field safety overpursue, cut back to the other hashmark and put the ball in the painted area.

If the previous clip was the No. 1 pick's best play of the game, the clip above is the best throw he made on the afternoon.

Seattle starts with a two-high look pre-snap before rotating the boundary safety into the hook-to-curl area to play Cover 3. That takes away the curl from Nailor on the curl-flat concept. Maybe Mendoza can hit Mayer on the flat route, but the linebacker manages to avoid the pick and stay on top of the route. So, that's a fine decision to hold onto the ball. But the problem is that the pocket starts to break down with Trey Zuhn III getting bull-rushed by Byron Murphy II.

Mendoza manages to get out of trouble, but he can settle down and pick his eyes up at the 10-yard line instead of continuing to scramble. That would have allowed him to find slot receiver Cody White earlier — who is wide open on the corner route with a coverage bust from Devon Witherspoon — and hit White with some room to run. Regardless, Mendoza eventually finds White and delivers a strike on the run for a 22-yard gain near the sideline.

This is where things started to get a little messy for the rookie, as the play above comes with about a minute left in the second quarter. Mendoza had a few missed opportunities for explosive plays in the game, with the one above being the biggest.

The Seahawks show a two-safety coverage pre-snap but rotate into Cover 3 with the boundary safety spinning down. Since the Raiders are in a three-by-one formation, the boundary corner is locked in man coverage against Tucker, the Silver and Black's best deep threat.

Tucker beats press coverage and has a couple of steps on the corner, while the field or deep safety isn't in a position to help the corner on a pass outside of the numbers. Mendoza gets to Tucker in his progression but doesn't pull the trigger. Maybe left guard Spencer Burford losing control of Murphy discouraged the quarterback from letting it rip, but he has enough time and a clean enough pocket to make that throw.

Instead, Mendoza opts to scramble and only picks up one yard. To be fair, this was the play that had the 4th and 1/first and 10 confusion (see the markers on the field and the scorebug on the top of the screen). So, maybe that played a factor in his decision, but this was certainly a missed opportunity.

Part of the reason Mendoza had such a low EPA is that he took six sacks on the afternoon. That was the result of some great play calling from Seattle's defensive mastermind/head coach Mike Macdonald, and the rookie quarterback's subpar feel for pressure.

This is a perfect play call by Macdonald. Vegas runs a play-action pass where the entire offensive line and the full back work left to sell the run fake, while running back Mike Washington Jr. inserts into the protection scheme on the right edge. Meanwhile, Seattle slants the defensive line to the strong side of the formation as the MIKE and WILL linebackers blitz, on top of the cornerback coming off the edge.

So, the Seahawks end up with a numbers advantage, where the Raiders have three blockers (Zuhn, right tackle DJ Glaze and Washington) to account for four pass-rushers (the edge, two linebackers and the corner). Also, Mendoza's back is turned to the defense, and Kubiak calls a shot play with two deep routes.

That being said, he gets turned around well before Witherspoon gets there and doesn't sense the pressure coming, failing to move off his spot. Again, this is a tough look — especially for a quarterback making his first start.

But if we back up to the pre-snap look, the safety playing outside the hashmark with the corner in press coverage was the tell that Witherspoon was blitzing, especially since the receiver is in a reduced or cut split (meaning between the numbers and hashmark). That creates a learning opportunity for the young QB.

Another sack that highlights how Macdonald tested Mendoza's ability to read the defense when the picture changes post-snap and handle pressure.

Seattle comes out in a double A-gap look with a seven-man front, where four pass-rush threats are on the weak side of the offensive line (in this instance, the offense's right side). So, the quarterback changes the protection, sliding it to the right. However, Macdonald doesn't run a blitz but rather a simulated pressure, where all four defenders on the right side drop into coverage, and the nickel cornerback rushes through the C-gap for a four-man rush.

Since the line is sliding right and there's an edge rusher outside of the tight end, left tackle Kolton Miller stays with Murphy in the protection call, and Mayer sticks with the edge rusher, leaving Witherspoon unblocked as a free rusher. Mendoza doesn't see or feel the pressure and ends up taking another big hit for a sack on third down.

To be fair, it looks like he was trying to throw hot to Ashton Jeanty. But Witherspoon closed so quickly that he had already started making the tackle by the time Jeanty got his head around. Still, this is another instance where Mendoza needs to expect pressure with the nickel as close to the line of scrimmage as he is pre-snap.

Finally, Mendoza had a few throws where his accuracy got away from him, and the one above really hurt.

On this play, it's 2nd and 10 with about 2:45 to play and the Raiders trailing by 11. Seattle keeps the coverage pretty vanilla (for Macdonald's standards, at least), playing Cover 6 with quarters to the wide side of the field near the goal line. Mendoza makes the right read since the safety steps inside while wide receiver Jack Bech runs an out route. That's open for a potential touchdown.

However, Mendoza doesn't finish the throw, so the pass sails on him and falls incomplete. Granted, the pocket is collapsing, but he had enough room to deliver an accurate pass and just missed the opportunity.

If you're looking for more plays from Mendoza's first start, dive into this thread I posted on X/Twitter.

#2657. Bears have a tough path to the playoffs, but are focused on 1-0

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country.

You don't focus on next week or the week after and who we got and prime times or the non-prime times."

"You focus on being prepared for that moment of when the the ball gets snapped the first time, whistle gets blown, and we focus on being 1-0 that week. And then when the next one comes up, we'll focus on being 1-0 that week. And if you go 1-0 each week and you focus on that each week, you'll turn out to kind of be where you want to be at the end of it."

Head coach Ben Johnson also met the media today, and it's not hard to figure out where Caleb's 1-0 mindset comes from.

When asked about his big-picture take on the NFC North, Johnson said, "It really doesn't matter right now. Once again, it's all about winning this week. #2655. The NFL officials who pulled double duty got double pay (as they should)

Some things go without saying. Nowadays, however, it’s sometimes important to state the obvious.

Via Mark Maske of Front Office Sports, the four officials who ended up officiating two games on Sunday (Don Willard, Terry Killens, Jabir Walker, and Justin Larrew) will get paid for working two games.

Why wouldn’t they? Getting twice the pay for twice the work should be a given. The real question is whether they should have gotten even more.

Folks who work overtime usually get time-and-a-half pay. In some instances, going above and beyond the call of duty results in double pay.

Here’s the real question — did the officials who were supposed to work one game in Week 10 but didn’t get still get their pay? Or do officials only get paid for the games they actually officiate, even if/when the NFL seemingly overreacts, reshuffles the deck, and cancels an official’s assignment that the official was otherwise ready and willing to fulfill?

It still seems that the NFL overreacted to the situation, turning the officiating assignments upside down in lieu of deciding to do whatever needed to be done to get the officials to their assigned game so that the existing crews wouldn’t be disrupted.

#2648. Despite the loss, Rockets Alperen Sengun continues his career-best shooting

When the Houston Rockets traded for Alperen Sengun in the 2021 NBA draft, they knew they were getting one of the best international players. An MVP of the Basketball Super League at 19, Sengun was already dominating overseas professional leagues.

Over the years, Sengun has gone from an up-and-coming young star to one of the best players in the NBA and a two-time All-Star. Throughout his NBA career, Sengun has also been one of the best post players in the NBA. He has shown he can score in the paint against the NBA's best defenders. Even with his scoring ability in the post, his offensive game has at times been limited by struggles not only in the mid-range but also from the 3-point range.

NBA teams are smart; they have multiple scouts and entire departments dedicated to knowing every strength and weakness of their opponents. Opposing teams quickly realized that if Sengun gets to his spot in the paint, it's usually too late to stop him. So teams started sagging off Sengun on pick-and-rolls, and whenever he got the ball away from the basket, they forced him to take a shot from outside.

That defensive strategy made life a lot harder for Sengun at times, as it became every opposing team's strategy when facing the Rockets. Sengun shot just 24.8% from the 3-point range in his first season, on 1.6 attempts. The next season, Sengun shot a higher percentage at .333 but at half the volume of the first season, as he sometimes hesitated on wide-open 3-pointers, choosing to pass on them and drive into a crowded paint.

Sengun's 3-point shooting dropped over the next two seasons from .333 to a career-worst .233 in his fourth season. Sengun has often said that is the one part of his offense that needs to improve if he wants to unlock his entire game. Sengun worked tirelessly on his 3-point shooting every summer, every practice, and before every game. Sengun has talked for years about his confidence in shooting 3-pointers, as he told SB Nation three years ago during training camp.

The hard work is starting to pay off in his sixth season, as Sengun is off to the best 3-point shooting start of his career.

HOUSTON, TEXAS – APRIL 24: Alperen Sengun #28 of the Houston Rockets shoots a three pointer during the first quarter of the game against the Los Angeles Lakers at Toyota Center on April 24, 2026 in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Sengun, now in his sixth season, is starting to translate all the hard work he puts into his 3-point shot into the game. Not only has Sengun improved his outside shooting, but he leads the Rockets in 3-point shooting at 48.1 percent. It is on only 2.1 attempts per game, but that is also a career-high for Sengun. A high volume of shots from downtown has never been Sengun's goal; it is more about him being a threat from long range, which opens up the court for the Rockets' center. It's not just that he is making 3-pointers; it's that he isn't hesitating from deep when teams play him for the drive.

Sengun has made a 3-pointer in a career-high six straight games and in eight of his last ten games. For Sengun, if he keeps improving from deep, teams will have to respect him from that range, which gives him more space; with his ability to handle the ball and his court vision, it could take his offensive game to an entirely different level.

With a reliable 3-point game and improved play on the defensive end, Sengun could be in serious contention for MVP votes at the end of the season. Pretty good for a player 16 other teams passed on in 2021.

#2642. Dillon Brooks’ intensity remains essential to the Suns’ identity

There are plenty of things in this world that you love 85% of the time and can't stand the other 15%. Group texts immediately come to mind. You love being part of the conversation, whether it's with family members, lifelong friends, or your sports buddies discussing the latest developments surrounding the Phoenix Suns. But sometimes those conversations go completely off the rails, your phone starts vibrating like it's sitting on a washing machine during the spin cycle, and you find yourself eternally grateful for whoever developed the technology to mute group text notifications.

As it pertains to the Phoenix Suns, the same could be said about Dillon Brooks.

We were baptized in the Dillon Brooks experience a season ago, and the overwhelming majority of the returns were positive. He's a culture setter and an attitude definer, somebody whose presence dictates the level of physicality with which your basketball team operates. Last season, he also showed us that he has considerably more tools in his offensive arsenal than many of us anticipated, averaging a career-high 20.2 points on 17.1 field-goal attempts per game.

But with that tenacity comes an edge, and navigating it without going over can be a delicate exercise. That's where the other 15% of the Dillon Brooks experience resides. The technical fouls. The flagrant fouls. The moments when the very characteristics that make him such a valuable member of your basketball team become the source of your frustration. And oftentimes, it's the timing of those infractions that makes them particularly maddening. Late-game situations and high-leverage possessions are instances in which discipline needs to supersede emotion, and Brooks doesn't always recognize when that transition needs to occur.

You love what he brings to your basketball team 85% of the time. The other 15%? You find yourself wishing Dillon Brooks had the same mute button as your group texts.

That being said, we've seen a different version of Dillon Brooks thus far this season. He's averaging 13.8 points on 12.0 shot attempts per game. Maybe it starts with the haircut, but whatever has changed, it's manifesting itself in his performance on the basketball court.

With the acquisition of Miles Bridges, Brooks has looked somewhat out of place to begin the season (as has Bridges). Much akin to the duplicative nature of Devin Booker and Jalen Green's skill sets, the same can be said of Brooks and Bridges. They occupy similar spaces on the floor and are asked to perform similar functions within the starting unit. Be a quality point-of-attack defender, knock down the three ball when called upon, and provide some physicality and assistance on the glass.

The Suns have found themselves in an interesting conundrum as the season has unfolded. There are instances when neither player appears entirely certain of where he should be positioned, whom he should be covering, or how to navigate switches on the defensive end. That uncertainty creates a particularly frustrating defensive dynamic because it compromises the very aggression that makes both players effective.

When they're aggressive, miscommunication leaves somebody exposed, and the opposition makes them pay for it. And then there are possessions when it appears they're being overly cautious, almost hesitant to do anything for fear of doing it wrong. That too burns them defensively. For two players whose effectiveness is predicated in large part on their physicality and assertiveness, indecision can be debilitating. It's difficult to impose your will on a basketball game when you're still trying to figure out where you're supposed to be.

This conundrum has contributed to the challenges the starting unit has faced throughout the early stages of the season. They're not a horrible offensive unit, primarily because Devin Booker's consistency has served as the rising tide that lifts the boats around him. Defensively, however, this group has yet to establish an identity. And when you juxtapose that against what we're experiencing from the second unit, a group that clearly understands its individual roles and how those roles complement one another, it becomes glaringly apparent how discombobulated the starting five has been.

Last night against the Denver Nuggets, we saw head coach Jordan Ott make an adjustment that appeared to unlock Dillon Brooks. That adjustment? He opened the second quarter with Brooks alongside members of the second unit, and almost immediately we saw Dillon being Dillon again.

Through his first three minutes as part of that lineup, Brooks attempted four shots. Granted, he went 1-of-4 from the field, but what stood out to me was the decisiveness with which he was operating. There was a familiarity to his approach, an aggressiveness that we'd grown to appreciate a season ago. He looked empowered to assert himself offensively without having to navigate the overlapping responsibilities that exist within the starting five.

The shots weren't necessarily falling, but the mentality was there. And from that point forward, Brooks delivered one of his best performances of the young season.

Now, I'm not about to head to my group text and flood its participants with messages advocating for Dillon Brooks to take 17 shots a night again. As Brooks has shown us throughout his career, his inefficiency can be his downfall. He attempted more shots than any member of the Phoenix Suns last night, going 6-of-17 from the field to get his 15 points. Not exactly great.

What this team needs more of is an engaged Dillon Brooks. Somebody who's emotionally invested in the game, actively disrupting what the opposition is attempting to accomplish, and embracing the alpha mentality that has become synonymous with his brand of basketball.

Brooks is the emotional leader of the starting unit, much like Jordan Goodwin is the emotional leader of the second unit. When Brooks is passive and isn't asserting himself, it affects his individual performance and, by extension, the performance of those around him. His intensity has a trickle-down effect on his teammates, and when that intensity is absent, you can feel it throughout the lineup.

Again, it's a fine edge to navigate. But it's one Brooks has navigated throughout his NBA career. It's his X factor, the characteristic that makes him special and gives him value beyond his statistical production.

Hell, he even picked up a horseshit technical foul last night after knocking down a three-pointer and barking at the opposing bench. Apparently, only Dillon Brooks can earn a technical foul for doing something we routinely see across the NBA. As frustrating as the whistle was, it was another indication of how engaged he was in the game.

It was his third technical foul of the season through 13 games, meaning he's averaging one every 4.3 games. That's a slightly more disciplined pace than a season ago, when he averaged one every 3.3 games en route to accumulating a league-leading 17 technical fouls.

The ideal balance, in my eyes, is a version of Brooks who takes somewhere around 11 shots per game, assumes greater offensive responsibility when sharing the floor with the second unit, and remains the emotional leader of the starting five. Defensively, you want him to take charge, communicate, dictate physicality, and impose his will, rather than operate with uncertainty and defer to those around him.

There's no perfect formula for finding that balance, particularly for a player whose greatest strength can occasionally become his greatest weakness. The Suns need Brooks to understand when to turn the volume up and when to dial it back. But they also need him to remain the emotional heartbeat of that starting unit. His aggression, physicality, and willingness to get under somebody's skin are part of what makes him valuable.

Give me an engaged Dillon Brooks, and I'll live with having to mute the group text from time to time. Now do me a favor, send this article to one of your friends via group text.

#2641. ESPN chief: Media coverage of Joe Buck, Troy Aikman dustup is "disappointing"

The Joe Buck vs. Troy Aikman Real Broadcasters of the NFL drama has added another layer of unexpected reality to the ultimate reality show that is pro football. Their mutual boss claims that ESPN doesn’t like the coverage of the situation.

“Joe and Troy have done a great job for us on Monday Night Football.” ESPN president Jimmy Pitaro said Tuesday at the SBJ Media Innovators conference, via Brandon Contes of Awful Announcing. “When I say ‘us,’ they’ve done a great job for ESPN, they’ve done a great job for the league, they’ve done a great job for the game, and most importantly, they’ve done a great job for fans.

“Are we happy about the media coverage recently? Of course not. It’s been disappointing. But these guys are professionals, and they’re delivering every week. If you watched it last night, another super high-quality production and telecast, and I’d fully expect that to continue that through the season and through the Super Bowl.”

At some level, they shouldn’t be disappointed. Any attention is, at some level, good attention. While it’s unlikely that anyone is tuning in for a Monday night game solely to witness the interactions of Buck and Aikman, it adds a little extra something to the overall buzz arising from the broadcast.

The deeper question is who Pitaro and the other big shots at ESPN are “disappointed” with. The situation didn’t come to light because everyone involved decided to keep the dirty laundry in house. People started talking privately. Aikman has said plenty publicly that confirms the situation and otherwise stirs the pot.

ESPN has no cause to be disappointed with those who did their jobs by pulling the threads of a genuinely interesting, uncontived, and in many ways unprecedented story. If the folks who write the checks should be miffed at anyone, it should be at the recipients of those checks who decided not to hold their own tongues in check regarding an obviously sensitive situation.

#2632. Dan Campbell won't wallow in "what ifs" arising from injuries

The Lions have, in recent weeks, lost both linebacker Jack Campbell (neck) and defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (knee) to significant injuries. Coach Dan Campbell won’t wallow in worrying about what may have been if the injuries hadn’t occurred.

“I think there’s times where, if you’re not careful, you lay in bed at night and you start thinking about all the ‘what ifs,’” Campbell told reporters on Tuesday. “And at some point, you just become a miserable piece of shit. And I’m not gonna do it, man. We’re not doing it.

“I refuse to look at it that way. Does it sting? Yeah, it sure did in the moment. It’s time to move on. We have to.

“And what has happened with Jack Campbell and with Hutch now will not be in vain. We can’t allow it to. They got us to this point. And so what are we gonna do about it, man? Are we just gonna let it go to waste, or are we gonna do something and pick up the slack?”

It’s the right attitude. Injuries happen. Sometimes, they happen to great players. (The more great players a team has, the greater the chances that one of them will be injured.)

The only approach is to tap the next man up on the shoulder, expect him to do his job to the best of his ability, not allow it to become a “woe is us” situation, and keep going.

That becomes easier, of course, if a team has quality depth. Which is why some teams that are top heavy with highly-paid stars find themselves in a pinch when those stars aren’t available to play.

"That offense is built around timing. If you threw Brock Purdy in there, he'd be a great fit for that offense. That's the type of quarterback. We haven't seen that (in Minnesota)," Hundley said.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Murray has started six games for Minnesota this season, completing 100 of 154 passes for 1,022 yards, five touchdowns and three interceptions. He owns an 86.6 passer rating and has added 167 rushing yards on 29 attempts. Minnesota went 5-1 in his six starts despite modest passing production.

Hundley believes Murray also entered a much different situation than the one he had as the No. 1 overall pick in Arizona.

"When you come in as the No. 1 pick, they will build the offense around you. Now you don't get that luxury. You come in and they say, 'We're running this. Do with it what you can. And if you can't succeed in this and lead us to where we want to go, we're going to find somebody else.' It's not that same pull when you come in as the No. 1 pick. So it's an interesting spot to be in."

Murray has also dealt with multiple injuries this season. He suffered a concussion in Minnesota's season opener before sustaining a hamstring strain following the Vikings' Week 8 loss to the Detroit Lions. O'Connell subsequently described Murray as "week to week," and the quarterback has not played since.

"I personally thought he was going to do a lot better when you look at the Vikings' past QB history of coming in and revamping their career. I said before the season I thought that would happen with Kyler, but I haven't seen what we're used to seeing with him," Hundley said.

Minnesota has since reunited with Kirk Cousins, acquiring him from the Las Vegas Raiders for a 2027 third-round pick. Cousins led the Vikings to a 30-10 victory over the Green Bay Packers in his first start back with the organization.

Cousins will make his second consecutive start when the Vikings (7-2) face the San Francisco 49ers (7-1) on Sunday night in Mexico City.

#2629. Hawks' CJ McCollum out at least 4 weeks with calf strain, putting rookie Kingston Flemings in the spotlight

Atlanta Hawks guard CJ McCollum has a left calf strain and will be sidelined for at least four weeks. The Hawks announced the injury update on Tuesday.

McCollum sustained the injury in Sunday's win over the Milwaukee Bucks. Imaging has since revealed the calf strain. He'll be reevaluated in four weeks, per the Hawks.

Through 14 games, McCollum is averaging 14.5 points, 3.9 assists, 3.1 rebounds and 1.1 steals per game while shooting 43.3% from the floor and 35.2% from 3. The Hawks enter Tuesday at 8-6, tied with the Miami Heat for the fourth-best record in the Eastern Conference.

The injury is a blow for the Hawks as they lose a key playmaker and their veteran voice on the court.

McCollum, 35, began the season as Atlanta's starting point guard. But he gave way to rookie Kingston Flemings in the starting unit, recently telling the NBA on Prime that he approached head coach Quin Snyder about making the lineup change.

"I didn't like the way we were playing as a unit, as a starting unit," McCollum said. "I think we were a little sluggish. I think we were lackluster from a ball movement standpoint.

"I think we were stagnant, and we have a lot of guys that can create and make plays. And I think for Kingston, he's a guy who gets downhill. He's got tremendous speed. He's learning and growing. And I think it gives him a chance to kind of develop, for us as a franchise and for us as an organization. …

"The way I play, I can get to it off the bench, I can get to it as a starter. I'm mature enough to be able to handle different roles, different minutes."

With McCollum sidelined, the keys to the offense will belong to Flemings, whom the Hawks selected with the No. 8 pick in June's draft out of Houston. In 12 games including five starts, Flemings is averaging 7.8 points, 4.1 assists, 2.5 rebounds and 0.7 steals in 21.5 minutes per game.

Flemings' shooting efficiency has stood out, especially for a rookie. He's shooting 51.4% from the field and 42.9% on 1.8 3-point attempts per game. He's done so in limited playing time as McCollum has continued to play heavy minutes off the bench.

Flemings has been day-to-day with back tightness, but was reportedly able to practice on Tuesday. He projects to have an opportunity to build on his success with increased volume and playing time in McCollum's absence.

The Hawks also announced Tuesday that second-year backup forward Asa Newell will miss at least four months with a plantar plate tear in his left great toe that required surgery. Newell was averaging 3.6 points and 2.6 rebounds in 11 minutes per game in five appearances this season.

#2627. Lions create practice squad spot, set stage for Wednesday roster moves

The Detroit Lions announced on Tuesday that they've released defensive lineman Ben Stille from the practice squad, creating a vacancy on the 17-man squad ahead of their week of preparation for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Stille, a 29-year-old veteran defensive lineman, was a standout during training camp this offseason, but he failed to make the 53-man roster. He was quickly signed to the practice squad and got the call-up for Detroit's Week 1 game, playing just nine defensive snaps.

Whiteside spent two months on the Lions' practice squad earlier this year.

On top of that, the Lions are expected to activate safety Kerby Joseph from the Physically Unable to Perform list to the 53-man roster on Wednesday, the final day of Joseph's 21-day evaluation window. If the Lions don't activate Joseph, he would be shut down for the year, but on Tuesday, coach Dan Campbell indicated that Joseph will not only be activated, but they expect him to have a significant role in Sunday's game against the Buccaneers.

"The plan is to get him going. I think we're going to let him play," Campbell said.

It's not clear how the Lions will create the roster spot for Joseph, but the easiest way would be to place Aidan Hutchinson on injured reserve after he suffered a torn ACL on Sunday.

The Bruins and Kings will both look to get back on track when they meet Tuesday night at TD Garden.

7:39 p.m.: Boston has not registered a shot on goal for a few minutes now. Minten shoots and misses just wide.

#2620. NBA trade rumors 2026-27: Dejounte Murray market lukewarm, what about Zion Williamson?

NBA front offices generally wait about 20 games to assess their teams before seriously looking into the trade market. Even more, it's not until Dec. 15, when many contracts signed over the summer become trade-eligible, that the market really heats up. That, however, never stops the NBA trade rumor mill, so here is the latest.

Soon after news broke of Dejounte Murray's agent requesting a trade for the point guard out of New Orleans, rumors tried to link Murray to the Phoenix Suns. There was some logic to it: The salaries line up and, at least outside the Valley of the Sun, the sense is Phoenix could use a point guard.

However, most of that speculation seemed to come out of Murray's camp, not Phoenix, which has limited interest in him, according to multiple reports, including Chris Manix here at NBC Sports. He also reports the market for Murray is "lukewarm." Actually, lukewarm may be putting it kindly. Here is what one "high ranking" NBA executive told Kelly Iko of Yahoo Sports:

"What a f****** mess. No one wants to touch him."

Coming off a torn Achilles that cost him most of two seasons, other teams see Murray as a distressed asset making $32.8 million this season, with a player option he almost certainly picks up for $30.8 million next season. Teams will want picks, likely a first-round pick, to take on that much money. Based on the history of Pelicans lead executive Joe Dumars in dealing with Trey Murphy III and Herb Jones (two players other teams actually want), this is going to drag out.

The Sacramento Kings are 1-12 and their coach, Doug Christie, is in the final year of his contract. On 29 teams in the league, that would be the definition of a coach on the hot seat, but in Sacramento they pushed back hard when the idea first came out, saying Christie was safe. He is a favorite of ownership there.

That hasn't completely changed. Marc Stein of The Stein Line reports the Kings "would prefer not to fire" Christie during the season to limit the amount of "tumult and upheaval" during Darius Acuff Jr.'s rookie campaign. Most likely, Christie is let go after the season. If/when that happens, two names to watch are Tom Thibodeau and Mark Jackson. Thibodeau (who has connections to GM Scott Perry) has coached more recently and had more success, while former Warriors coach Mark Jackson is a favorite of owner Vivek Ranadive from those days in Golden State.

In other Sacramento news, they are still interested in adding veteran point guard Gabe Vincent as a backup behind Acuff, he has a standing offer, Stein reports. That he hasn't jumped at the deal could be telling.

• With all the Pelicans trade talk right now, would they consider trading Zion Williamson? Maybe, but the return isn't going to be as robust as they might hope, reports ESPN's Tim MacMahon on the Hoop Collective podcast: "He's somewhere on the LaMelo (Ball) to Ja (Morant) spectrum, in terms of trade value." Ball went for a first-round pick and Naz Reid, plus three pick swaps, and MacMahon is saying Williamson would get a smaller return than that. Morant was traded for Jerami Grant and Kris Murray.

• While the Miami Heat have found a groove of late, this is a team known to be looking for upgrades, and Ira Winderman of the Sun Sentinel suggests to watch out for Zach LaVine as a target.

• The Indiana Pacers may be in the market to trade for a wing, but they want to get Tyrese Haliburton back healthy and let things shake out first, Stein reports.

#2619. Jerry Jones makes surprising statement about 49ers takeover

One of the biggest shockers from the 49ers' 46-40 road victory against the Cowboys on Sunday was the takeover of AT&T Stadium by San Francisco fans.

Cowboys owner Jerry Jones appeared on "105.3 The Fan" on Tuesday morning and was asked his reaction to 49ers fans filling up his stadium and said, "That was not a shocker."

Jerry Jones downplays 49ers fans taking over AT&T Stadium on Sunday. AP Photo/Jeff Roberson

"Well, I don't know if you saw the price of those tickets that they were paying … but it was unbelievable," Jones said. "I would say the highest price of any ticket."

Jones said the 49ers have "always had a way above-average attendance to our away games here in Dallas" and that longtime Cowboys season ticket holders blamed "this secondary market."

Jerry Jones meeting with members of the media following Sunday's game against the 49ers. AP Photo/Jeffrey McWhorter

"Many of our fans have seats licensed. So they technically own those seats," Jones said. "For the most part, fans that have been out there for years, and years, and years. A lot of times, our ticket holders will maybe take two or three key games of the year and sell those tickets."

While Jones insisted that Cowboys fans price-gouged 49ers fans for their tickets, Dallas has certainly enjoyed a large turnout by its fans this season.

According to ESPN, Dallas ranks first in the NFL for attendance, averaging 91,766 fans per home game. San Francisco averages 71,131 fans per home game.

After the game, Jones was asked about the 49ers fans' invasion and gave a defensive response: "We have a lot of [Cowboys fans] on the road ourselves."

San Francisco 49ers fans seen filling up AT&T Stadium during Sunday's game. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

That is accurate, too. ESPN reported that Dallas has averaged 73,450 fans per road game.

Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott was also aware of the sea of red in the seats and told reporters he "[t]ricked myself, told myself early the red was for my high school."

Prescott applauded the 49ers Faithful. "Their fans were more present than ours. But it created a great atmosphere, so take the good out of it one way or another. Leave it there."

San Francisco's fans impacted Prescott's offense, forcing Dallas to utilize a silent count.

#2609. NFL news, live updates: Aidan Hutchinson reportedly suffers torn ACL on sack celebration; Patriots QB Drake Maye out indefinitely with ankle injury

Another NFL Sunday is in the books, with just one game left in Week 10 as the Baltimore Ravens host the LA Chargers on "Monday Night Football."

Sunday kicked off with a bang as the Detroit Lions and New England Patriots faced off in Munich, Germany, with injuries to two stars that will have all eyes drawn as the new week plays out. Lions star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson suffered what is feared to be a season-ending ACL tear while celebrating a sack against Patriots quarterback Drake Maye … who suffered an ankle injury on that very sack, which knocked him out of the game and could cost him the season.

Week 10 also offered us our first look at Las Vegas Raiders No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza as a starter. He led scoring drives on each of the Raiders' first two possessions and entered halftime with a 10-7 lead over the Seattle Seahawks, but Drew Lock rallied with two passing touchdowns in the third quarter to take the lead, improving to 3-0 as a starter for Seattle this season. Raiders star tight end Brock Bowers exited the loss with an ankle injury.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more coming out of Week 10.

NFL Network's Ian Rapoport gave an update on some injuries to watch on Tuesday. It is still early in the practice week, but Rapoport mainly spoke about Kenneth Walker III and Baker Mayfield.

Walker missed last week's game due to a groin injury, but rookie Emmett Johnson balled out, so the Chiefs may not be rushing Walker back to the field.

Mayfield is coming off a bye, but was spotted in a walking boot last week at the facility. Rapoport said that he thinks Mayfield could miss this week's game, in which undrafted rookie QB Jalon Daniels would be back under center for Tampa Bay.

The Tennessee Titans are adding wide receiver Wan'Dale Robinson to injured reserve due to an ankle injury, per team reporter Jim Wyatt.

In a corresponding move, the team is signing wide receiver Xavier Restrepo to the active roster.

Robinson suffered the ankle injury in the team's Week 10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars and could not return to the game. Restrepo was activated from the practice squad on game day and finished with 31 yards on three receptions.

Robinson has played in all nine games for Tennessee this season. He has brought in 38 receptions for 272 yards and a team-high three receiving touchdowns.

Head coach Robert Saleh has not revealed the extent of Robinson's ankle injury. If the wideout returns this season, he would first be eligible to be activated off IR in Week 15, ahead of the team's game against the Indianapolis Colts.

Tennessee will be without Robinson for at least the games against the Dallas Cowboys, Jacksonville Jaguars, Washington Commanders, and Detroit Lions.

Miami Dolphins defensive tackle Jordan Phillips suffered a torn biceps in last week's loss to the Indianapolis Colts that will sideline the 2025 fifth-round pick for the remainder of the season, according to ESPN's Marcel Louis-Jacques.

Phillips is the third Miami DT to sustain a season-ending injury in the past two weeks, per Louis-Jacques.

The Dolphins are 1-8 under first-year head coach Jeff Hafley. That said, their young core has flashed promise, especially on the defensive side of the ball.

The Commanders announced Tuesday that they are opening the 21-day practice window for running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt.

He has been sidelined due to a groin injury since Week 5. The running back remains on IR and must be activated before he can play in a game for Washington.

The Commanders take on the Cincinnati Bengals this week for "Monday Night Football," giving JCM an extra day of rest to get up to speed.

Croskey-Merritt has had a rather unproductive season so far, but at times has shown how effective he can be. Through five games, he has 239 yards and two touchdowns on 67 carries.

The NFL has utilized another flex to switch around the Week 12 schedule, per ESPN's Adam Schefter.

The New England Patriots and the Los Angeles Chargers were previously scheduled for that week's "Sunday Night Football" matchup.

With the injury to Patriots QB Drake Maye, and the Chargers' 1-8 start, the NFL has moved the game out of primetime.

New England-Los Angeles will now kick at 4:05 p.m. ET. Moving the Titans and Jaguars game into a 1 p.m. ET kick.

The new SNF kick will feature the Las Vegas Raiders taking on the Cleveland Browns.

The bye week came at a good time for Chicago. Wide receiver Luther Burden III was placed in the league's concussion protocol following the team's last game against the Buccaneers.

Coming out of the bye week, though, ESPN's Courtney Cronin reports that Burden has cleared concussion protocol.

Cronin also added that Kyler Gordon is considered "day-to-day" by head coach Ben Johnson due to a shoulder injury also suffered against the Buccaneers.

The Texans are on a short week this week, taking on the Colts on Thursday night in an AFC South divisional matchup.

It's a tough time for Houston to not have many days to get some much-needed rest, as the Texans are looking like they could be down some impactful players.

KPRC2 Houston's Aaron Wilson reported on Tuesday that defensive end Danielle Hunter, RB Woody Marks and WR Marvin Harrison Jr. are currently expected to miss Thursday night's game.

The good news for Texans fans is that running back David Montgomery was practicing, and it looks like he is in a good spot to start Thursday night for the first time since injuring his groin in Week 5.

The Cleveland Browns have been through this type of season before. It has just been a long time.

In 1979, the Browns had seven fourth-quarter drives to win games. In the 1980 season they were 11-5 and nine of the wins came by one score. That group got the nickname of the Kardiac Kids. Brian Sipe became a Cleveland legend, and won the 1980 NFL MVP award.

The 2026 Browns aren't at that level yet, but they're getting close. After rallying to beat the Houston Texans on a touchdown with 53 seconds left, the Browns are the first team in NFL history to win each of its first six games by four or fewer points, according to ESPN Insights. Every one of those wins has included a game-winning drive in the fourth quarter. It has been a magical, improbable run.

Al-Shaair suffered a groin injury in Week 3 that has kept him out of Week 4 and Week 10. He will reportedly require surgery, but he has not been ruled out for the season as of now.

The Texans have been hit with injuries at various points this season. Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring), Danielle Hunter (hamstring) and David Montgomery (groin) were among those who also missed Week 10. Montgomery has not played since Week 5.

Through seven games, the 29-year-old Al-Shaair has 26 solo tackles and 58 total tackles, plus three pass deflections.

Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell won't let one freak injury change how he approaches the game. Following star pass rusher Aidan Hutchinson tearing his ACL during a celebration, Campbell said he will not discourage other Lions players from celebrating big plays moving forward.

Campbell, who made those comments during an appearance on Detroit's 97.1 The Ticket, explained that Hutchinson's injury was "just one of those things," and that's not enough for Campbell to establish a "nobody celebrates anymore" rule.

"I hate it, I know he hates it. But I mean, the number of moves that I've seen Hutch make and the number of plyometrics, explosive movements, the spins, the one-leg lateral movements, lateral balances, I'm just like, it was one of those things, man," Campbell said. "I hate it. I think we all understand what it is, and let's be smart, but no, I'm not gonna say, 'Nobody celebrates anymore.'"

When asked whether he felt he would need to address the issue with the team, Campbell shot down that idea. He then revealed that he once sustained an injury while celebrating a big play.

The Vikings and Raiders' playoff hopes are trending in different directions.

Minnesota's chances of advancing to the postseason improved to 90% with its Sunday win, per Next Gen Stats, even as it sits in second place in a crowded NFC North. The Raiders' chances fell to 10% after their loss, their 4-6 record paired with their remaining schedule projecting worse chances than also-currently-out-of-it AFC contenders in the New England Patriots, Baltimore Ravens and Houston Texans.

A similarity between the two teams whose fates will be tied this season by their shared Cousins custody: the expectation of evolution as the offensive cast settles into its roles.

There are quarterbacks like Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes, who achieve stardom and become synonymous with one team. There are quarterbacks like … well, we don't need to name them, but quarterbacks who never capitalize on their draft-day promise and fade into the ether. And then there's Kirk Cousins, whose career has swooped and swerved in a way he never can on the field.

From spare-parts draft pick to decade-long starter, from chain-wearing goof to one of the highest-paid players in the history of the sport, Cousins' career is a study in improbability, and naturally, he's just landed in the unlikeliest position of all — on track for true postseason success. You like that?

Jones would not elaborate with the hosts about the discussions regarding the Cowboys' defense and Parker's standing within the organization.

Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheim didn't directly support Parker on Monday, one day after a brutal showing from the Dallas defense in its 46-40 loss to the San Francisco 49ers.

Instead, he said everything is still under review.

"We're still working through the process, talking to the guys is the first step," Schottenheimer said, via The Dallas Morning News. "At the end of the day, there's a lot of things that we need to clean up as a football team. That starts with me."

The 26-year-old Joseph has not played this season due to a knee injury that limited him to only six games last season.

Barring a setback, Joseph, a 2024 First-team All-Pro, will be on the field when the Lions take on the Buccaneers in Week 11.

Dallas Cowboys right guard Tyler Booker sustained a high ankle sprain during the second quarter of Sunday's 46-40 loss to the San Francisco 49ers and is expected to miss at least four weeks, according to several reports.

Such an injury usually requires a recovery timeline of four to six weeks, but the Cowboys are hopeful that Booker can return in three to four weeks.

Starting cornerback DaRon Bland also suffered a right high ankle sprain during the Cowboys' first defensive series while trying to tackle 49ers receiver Deebo Samuel Sr. He had dealt with an injury to his left ankle during the previous week of practice.

The team is also considering whether or not to put both plalyers on injured reserve with a possible four-week absence. However, Dallas has a bye for Week 14, which could allow them to stay on the active roster.

The Chicago Bears should have running back Kyle Monangai available for Sunday's game against the New Orleans Saints.

Monangai has been out for more than a month with both a thumb injury and turf toe.

"It's something I can manage now," he said, via ESPN's Courtney Cronin. "The time off was needed though for sure. I feel in a much better spot than I was a month ago."

The two big Super Bowl odds movers this week resulted from one play on Sunday, when Aidan Hutchinson sacked Drake Maye and then Hutchinson proceeded to injure himself on the celebration.

Unfortunately, for the Lions, it's reportedly a torn ACL for Hutchinson, which would sideline him for the rest of the season. Detroit, despite a 7-2 record, moved from 18-1 to 20-1 odds to win the Super Bowl (11th-best odds). It's also reportedly a "significant lower-leg injury" for Maye, and with a 5-5 record already in a crowded AFC field, New England's Super Bowl odds tumbled from 28-1 entering the week to 66-1.

The Chargers are bringing in some reinforcements ahead of a Monday night clash against the Ravens. The team announced Monday that they have activated tight end David Njoku and linebacker Denzel Perryman from injured reserve.

Njoku has been marked out with a fibula injury, while Perryman has been out with a pectoral injury. Both players were listed as "questionable" heading into this weekend, but were full participants in practice on Saturday.

In related moves, Los Angeles placed guard/tackle Branson Taylor on IR and elevated defensive lineman Myles Adams from the practice squad.

The 0-8 Chargers are trying to pick up their first win of the year against Baltimore.

The Raiders have some good news on star tight end Brock Bowers, who exited Sunday's loss to the Seahawks with an ankle injury. Though the injury, which occurred during the first quarter, initially appeared concerning, Las Vegas head coach Klint Kubiak said Monday that things were better than originally feared.

In a press conference, Kubiak said that the team was "still evaluating" Bowers, but that the tight end will be day-to-day with the injury.

"It's not as bad as we thought, but still is a significant injury, so we'll keep monitoring him," Kubiak said.

Bowers, who missed the first two games of the season after undergoing minor knee surgery, leads Las Vegas in receiving with 676 yards and six touchdowns in eight games.

New York Jets head coach Aaron Glenn was hired by the team thanks to his excellence as a defensive coordinator. But after the team struggled on defense during Glenn's first year as head coach, he decided to take over defensive play-calling duties in 2026.

That change lasted just nine games. Glenn told reporters Monday he gave up defensive play-calling ahead of the team's 31-12 loss to the Buffalo Bills in Week 10, per ESPN.

Glenn said the move was made to help the team win games. He added that while Jets defensive coordinator Brian Duker called plays Sunday, Glenn was "very involved" in the team's scheme.

"I've said this and I will continue to do this: Anything I can do as a head coach to help us win games, I'm willing to do it," Glenn said. "I'm not afraid to do that. So I gave him the lead, but I was very involved in what we ran."

The change appeared positive initially, as the Jets (2-8) gave up just 10 points in the first half Sunday. But Buffalo's offense got rolling in the second half, allowing the team to pull away.

The Jets ultimately gave up 31 points in a loss to the Bills. Though, in Duker's defense, facing Josh Allen in your first game as a defensive play-caller is among the toughest asks in the NFL. The Bills rank first in the NFL with 31.9 points scored per game. In that sense, Duker's defense actually held the team under its season-long average … barely. The Jets still allowed 31 points, so the team shouldn't start popping the champagne just yet.

#2608. Jaylen Brown to miss 76ers game Wednesday vs. Magic due to 'hamstring strain'

The Philadelphia 76ers will take on the Orlando Magic on Wednesday night, but without star shooting guard Jaylen Brown.

He is dealing with a hamstring strain and has already been ruled out for tomorrow night's game. Brown picked up the injury during Philadelphia's win over the Brooklyn Nets on Monday.

The guard is in his first season with the 76ers after the infamous trade that sent him to Philadelphia from Boston. Brown has played in 14 games so far this season and is averaging 22.6 points, 6.6 rebounds, and 3.6 assists.

The Philadelphia guard had a slow start with his new team, scoring 19 points in his team debut. The 76ers have tried to find the best fit among Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, Brown, and free-agent signee LeBron James.

It finally seemed to be clicking for Brown ahead of the injury. He logged back-to-back games with 31 points, his season high. The guard finished Monday night's win with a double-double: 31 points and 13 rebounds. He shot just 47.4% from the field, but he made 10 of 11 attempts from the charity stripe as Philadelphia beat Brooklyn 135-123.

Without Brown in the lineup, the 76ers will likely give more minutes to Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Jabari Walker.

Wednesday's game against Orlando will be Brown's second missed game this season. He also missed Philly's first game of a back-to-back against the New York Knicks.

Brown was dealing with both a head and a hamstring injury coming out of Monday's win against Brooklyn. After the game, he said that he may have to get imaging done on Tuesday. Brown has been diagnosed with a left hamstring strain, but it remains unclear whether it will keep him out beyond Wednesday's game.

Philadelphia has the Magic, Milwaukee Bucks, Portland Trail Blazers, Miami Heat, and Indiana Pacers in its next five games.
